intro: You have come to Karahan Tepe, a mound in Şanlıurfa province, and to one of the oldest chapters of the human story: the 10th millennium BC. This is a pre-pottery Neolithic sanctuary, built before people had even learned to fire clay. Its T-shaped pillars and sculptures have earned it a fitting nickname — Göbekli Tepe's 'sister site'.
history: The site was first identified in 1997 by Bahattin Çelik, and since 2019 it has been excavated under the Taş Tepeler, or Stone Hills, Project. Pause for a moment and consider what you are looking at. These monumental structures date to the 10th–9th millennium BC, and they were raised by hunter-gatherers. They show that such communities could organise complex building work and shared ritual long before the first farming villages.
structure-2: Here are the circular enclosures. These round-planned cult enclosures house T-shaped pillars, the great hallmark of the Taş Tepeler period. Imagine the people who gathered inside these rings, surrounded by standing stones.
structure-3: Now look at the rock-cut basins. They were carved straight into the bedrock, and they are thought to have served ritual purposes. What was poured into them, and why, we can only wonder.
structure-4: And now, the anthropomorphic statues: human-shaped figures of stone. They are among the earliest monumental examples of the Neolithic era — some of the first times people carved themselves on this scale.
structure-5: This is the structure with a stone bench. Stone benches run inside the building, and it was used as a gathering place. Picture people seated side by side here, talking, listening, deciding together.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the T-shaped pillars, rising here as they did when they were first set up.
facts: Did you know? Locals call the site 'Keçilitepe'. The 2.3 m seated male statue found in 2023 is among the earliest realistic human sculptures known. Karahan Tepe is a contemporary of Göbekli Tepe. In the main chamber, eleven pillars were left standing out of the bedrock itself, and a human head emerges from the wall. The site is one of the hubs of the 'Taş Tepeler' research programme, which covers similar sites across the region — and only a small part of it has been dug so far.
outro: This brings our tour of Karahan Tepe to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have kept their secrets for a very long time; let them keep them for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
